correctness.rationale: The private-neighborhood proof exhausts all support patterns. A one-part set is independent, hence each selected vertex is self-private. If a set meets multiple parts, any selected vertex has positive degree inside the selected subgraph and must use an external private vertex. Complete-multipartite adjacency forces all other selected vertices into that private vertex's part; applying the argument from the opposite part forces exactly one selected vertex in each of two parts, and the two required omitted private vertices force both parts to have size at least two. This proves the classification. Maximality and both polynomials follow by direct counting. Literal exhaustive reconstruction through order 9 agrees on every tested subset.

evidence: Alon–Defant, arXiv:1904.02595, Theorem 1.3: for a direct product of \(n\) complete multipartite graphs, every irredundant set is an independent set plus a set of size at most \(2^n\); their main equality theorem concerns direct products of balanced complete multipartite graphs.
Their full text defines \(\operatorname{IR}(G)\) and states the direct-product host explicitly, so the object is not a single complete multipartite graph unless \(n=1\).
broader_coverage.reasoning: The direct-product theorem is broader in host construction but weaker in the one-factor implication: at \(n=1\) it only bounds the non-independent residue by two vertices. It does not force those two vertices to lie in distinct non-singleton parts, does not classify maximal irredundant sets, and does not count all irredundant sets. Therefore it does not dominate the retained claim.

originality.rationale: The retained claim is the exact all-set and maximal-set classification, plus both irredundance counting polynomials, for a single arbitrary complete multipartite graph. The closest inspected full-text theorem is Alon–Defant Theorem 1.3 for direct products: in a product of \(n\) complete multipartite factors an irredundant set decomposes into an independent part and at most \(2^n\) exceptional vertices. For one factor that permits up to two exceptional vertices but does not identify the exact cross-pair obstruction, maximal sets, or counting polynomials. Foundational sources define irredundance and general parameter relations. Exact semantic searches returned no statement-equivalent published finding.
residual_risks: The full 1979 foundational article was not available in the inspected lawful sources, so an unexposed family-specific statement in older literature remains a bibliographic risk.
Older literature may use private-neighbor or domination-chain terminology without the word “irredundance polynomial”; exact search cannot prove absence.

The scalar equality \(\operatorname{IR}(G)=\alpha(G)\) for one complete multipartite factor is compatible with later direct-product theory; originality is assigned to the exact all-set and maximal-set classification and the two enumerators, not merely to that scalar equality.

value.rationale: This is a natural complete classification for a foundational domination-chain invariant on a canonical graph family. It determines every irredundant set and every maximal irredundant set, hence both standard counting polynomials and both extremal irredundance numbers. The result also sharpens the one-factor case suggested by the later direct-product decomposition: the allowed two-vertex residue is identified exactly as a transversal between non-singleton parts. This is structural information useful for maximal-irredundant-set enumeration and reconfiguration questions, rather than an arbitrary finite slice or a mere recomputation of a known scalar.
